title: Advice on jazz education and his parents
summary: He favors getting records and playing, but advises a degree and masters for a teaching job; his parents backed education.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Right. If a parent comes to you and they have a son or daughter who is an aspiring musician and has got some talent and they say should I let my son or daughter try to go into jazz, has that ever happened to you?

Not really. What I would say is, honestly, what I would say is I would say if they wanted to get into jazz, if that’s what they want to do, and you’re worried about it, even though I’m really not a big proponent of jazz education in college, because I feel like if you really want to be a jazz musician the key to that is just getting the records that you love and learn them, and go out and play. The problem is going out and playing the part is so diminished these days that it’s not really, you know, I’m not sure that’s the best for a good kid. So what I would say would be this: have him go to school and get a music degree and get a masters. Because then they can have a teaching job and still play. And I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-

had many friends of mine in college, they’re tenured, they’re in the school, they have a tenured job, they have a pension happening, but they still go out and do gigs, they do their thing, they write and they’re still growing as musicians. And I think if I was to give them advice, that would be the advice. Get a degree and get a masters. And then they’d be set. And you know what? Depending on how talented they are it doesn’t even have to be in music. It could be in anything. But I would say definitely get the papers. But if you want a degree, if you want a job in music you have to have a masters.
Did your parents tell you that, try to tell you that?

My parents were very, you know they backed me up in whatever I wanted to do. It was a different time. You know I actually went to school to play basketball. And they just wanted me to graduate. They wanted me to do well in school and graduate, which was really good advice. Because the times when I did slip a little bit, I think I was on probation one semester, you know they got down on me a little bit. So yeah, they definitely were strong for me to get an education. The music thing I think when I was younger they were like thrilled by that, but I think as I got older they were less thrilled because I think they saw the reality of the jazz situation. But I didn’t have [inaudible].
